extracted.intended_audience: educators teaching news literacy and their students
extracted.subtask_description: Introduce and apply core standards journalists use to produce accurate, fair, and useful reporting; help students evaluate the credibility of information and practice newsroom decision-making. Used as a classroom resource (Checkology lesson/poster) for K–12 news literacy instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce the most accurate information possible; be as fair and accurate as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general purpose behind the standards is to produce the most accurate, fair and useful information possible. Accuracy is described as an aspirational standard that requires judgment and discussion to apply. Errors should prompt reconsideration and revision of practices to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness / Eliminate bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to eliminate bias and ensure reporting is fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness is aspirational and requires judgment. Determining fairness may involve discussion about balance, context, and how sources and perspectives are presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness / Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide information that is useful to the audience (serve the public's informational needs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal of journalism standards includes producing useful information; usefulness is considered alongside accuracy and fairness in evaluating quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fabrication / Prohibition against making things up
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invent facts, quotes, or events; fabrication is an obligatory violation of journalistic standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some standards are obligatory (such as the prohibition against making things up). This is presented as a non-negotiable rule distinct from aspirational standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anonymous sources / Attribution policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow newsroom policies governing when and how to use anonymous sources and attribute information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some standards are quantifiable (such as newsroom policies about the use of anonymous sources). Transparency about sourcing and consistent application of attribution rules are implied best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply judgment to determine whether a topic or event merits coverage as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing newsworthiness is listed as an area requiring judgment and discussion; it is part of applying aspirational standards in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating sources / Source verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the credibility of sources and verify information before publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating sources is highlighted as a judgment-based standard students should learn to apply; examples of adapting source-finding (e.g., using social media) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to correct errors and revise practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsider and revise standards and practices to prevent the recurrence of errors and improve reporting quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that standards are subject to constant reconsideration and revision — whether to prevent the recurrence of an error or to adapt to new tools and methods of gathering and reporting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to new tools/methods while maintaining standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply core standards when using new tools or methods (e.g., social media sourcing, livestreaming) and adapt verification practices accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include using social media to locate sources or livestreaming breaking news events. Standards should be adapted to new workflows and technologies without sacrificing accuracy, fairness, or verification.
